opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it actually came out of a very practical problem. After I left Google, Alexander Skidanov and I started NEAR.ai, and the original idea was program synthesis: teaching machines to write code from natural language descriptions. To do that well, you need a lot of training data: pairs of descriptions and code, solutions to small programming tasks, and so on.

So we built a crowdsourcing setup where people around the world would do these tasks for us, and a lot of them were students in places like China, Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia. And paying them turned out to be surprisingly painful. Some didn't have bank accounts that worked with the services we used, PayPal wasn't available in some countries, international wires had fees that were bigger than the payment itself, which was often a few dollars. So the cost of moving the money was dominating the actual work.

The natural thought was: okay, this is exactly what blockchain was supposed to solve, right? Global, permissionless, cheap value transfer. So we looked at what existed at the time, this was around 2018, and honestly nothing really worked for our use case. Fees on Ethereum were spiking, throughput was very limited, and the developer and user experience was really hard. You couldn't hand a student a wallet with seed phrases and gas mechanics and expect it to just work.

And as systems people, me coming from TensorFlow and Alex from MemSQL working on sharded databases, we looked at it and said, this is fundamentally a scaling and usability problem, and we know how to build sharded distributed systems. So we decided to pivot and build the protocol ourselves, with sharding for scalability and a big focus on usability: human-readable account names, low predictable fees, the ability for apps to cover costs for users.

What's funny is that it's come full circle. Now with AI agents and with questions around who owns data and how contributors get compensated, that original problem of paying people globally for their contributions to AI is more relevant than ever. So in a way, we went on a long detour to build the infrastructure we needed for the AI work in the first place.

r001.rationale: It describes contributors lacking usable bank accounts or PayPal, costly international wires, and the team turning to blockchain for global, low-cost value transfer.

r002.rationale: It says Ethereum fees were spiking, but does not state that blockchain transaction fees were around a dollar or otherwise dollar-scale and unsuitable for the small contributor payments.

r003.rationale: It says they built the protocol to provide the payment infrastructure needed for their AI work and describes this as a detour to build infrastructure for that work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the backstory is that NEAR actually started as NEAR.ai, and the whole idea was program synthesis, teaching machines to write code from natural language. This was 2017, 2018, and we needed a lot of training data. We needed people to write code, annotate it, describe what it does, and so on. So we built a crowdsourcing platform, and we had a lot of contributors coming from places like China, Eastern Europe, India, students who were happy to do this work for relatively small amounts of money.

And then we hit this very mundane problem, which is that we couldn't pay them. If you're trying to send ten dollars to a student in Ukraine or in China, the payment rails just don't work. The bank fees eat the whole amount, PayPal isn't available or gets blocked, and the compliance overhead for a small startup is enormous. So we looked at crypto, because on paper that's exactly what it's for, programmable money that moves across borders.

But when we actually tried it, it was unusable. The fees on Ethereum at the time could be higher than the payment itself, confirmation times were slow, and the user experience required people to understand private keys and gas and all of that. We're trying to pay someone who just wants to earn a bit of money on the side, and we're asking them to become a cryptography expert first.

So Alex and I kind of stepped back and asked, why is this so hard? And we ended up going down the rabbit hole of looking at the architecture of these systems. Our background is from Google, from building large distributed systems, and it was pretty clear that the way these blockchains were designed, every node processing every transaction, fundamentally couldn't scale to something like a payments use case for millions of people. And the developer and user experience was an afterthought.

At some point we realized the thing we actually wanted to build, which was a way for people anywhere in the world to be paid for contributing data or work, needed infrastructure that didn't exist. So the decision was, do we wait for someone else to build it, or do we build it ourselves? And we're engineers, so we started building. That became NEAR Protocol, with sharding for scalability, and a big focus on usability, things like human-readable account names and being able to onboard someone without them ever seeing a seed phrase.

The irony, of course, is that we spent several years on the infrastructure and then came back to the AI side, which is where we are now. But it really did start from that very practical problem of trying to pay people for coding data.

r001.rationale: Describes payment barriers across countries, including bank fees and unavailable or blocked PayPal, then says the team explored crypto for cross-border payments.

r002.rationale: States Ethereum fees could be higher than the small payment itself, making it impractical to pay contributors.

r003.rationale: Says they built NEAR because the payment infrastructure they needed did not exist, and later returned to the AI side.

astra-6.text:
Well, we didn’t start out trying to build a blockchain. We were working on an AI system that could help people write code, and we needed training data. The idea was to have contributors around the world provide examples and get paid for that work.

That brought up a practical problem: how do you send small payments to people in different countries without making the fees and onboarding more expensive than the work itself? Crypto looked like a natural fit. But as we explored it, we ran into limitations around scalability, transaction costs, and usability.

So it wasn’t that paying contributors inherently required a new protocol. It was that the infrastructure we wanted to build on didn’t seem ready for the application we had in mind. We started looking at that infrastructure problem, and that became the focus of NEAR.

r001.rationale: It says contributors were in different countries and that payment fees and onboarding could outweigh the small payments, prompting the team to consider crypto.

r002.rationale: It says fees could exceed the value of the work, but does not identify dollar-scale blockchain transaction fees.

r003.rationale: It says the infrastructure problem became NEAR’s focus, but does not state that NEAR was meant to solve payments so the team could return to its AI work.

sol-6.1.text:
We didn’t start out trying to build a blockchain. We were working on NEAR.ai, exploring how to teach machines to write code, and we needed people to contribute training examples. Then we ran into a very practical problem: how do you pay contributors around the world, especially when each contribution might earn only a small amount?

Traditional payment systems had fees and geographic restrictions that made that difficult. Cryptocurrency looked like a natural solution, but when we started looking at existing blockchains, we found that the cost, scalability, and usability weren’t where we needed them to be.

So the question became, what would it take to build infrastructure that could actually support an application like ours? We had experience with distributed systems, and that eventually led us to building NEAR Protocol. The blockchain wasn’t the original goal—it grew out of trying to solve a problem for the application.

r001.rationale: It says contributors were worldwide and traditional payment systems had geographic restrictions, prompting the team to consider cryptocurrency as a solution.

r002.rationale: It says existing blockchains had unsuitable cost, but does not state that transaction fees were around a dollar per transaction.

r003.rationale: It says NEAR grew from solving the application’s infrastructure problem, but does not say the goal was to return to the team’s AI work.
